title: Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?
keyPoints: In a named JPMS module, permitted subtypes may be in different packages of the same module.
On the classpath (unnamed module), all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type.
A sealed hierarchy can never span two different modules, regardless of configuration.
The module boundary is the strongest encapsulation: an outside module can never inject a permitted subtype.
Modularising unlocks a cleaner package layout for sealed hierarchies while keeping them closed.
The rule is checked at compile time and re-validated by the JVM at load time via the `PermittedSubclasses` attribute.

s1_definition.oneliner: Same module, different packages is allowed; classpath requires the same package; different modules is never allowed.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Same named module** – permitted subtypes may be in different packages of that module, because the module boundary provides strong encapsulation.
- **Classpath (unnamed module)** – all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type, because the package is the only encapsulation unit.
- **Cross-module** – never allowed; a sealed hierarchy cannot span two different modules.
- **Compile-time and load-time** – the rule is enforced by the compiler and re-validated by the JVM's `PermittedSubclasses` attribute check.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's head office declares the closed list of account products. If the whole bank operates as one unified organisation (a module), head office may place the approved products in different departments (packages) across that organisation. But if the bank is just a loose collection of branches with no central organisation (the classpath), head office can only approve products kept in the very same department as the master policy document. And an approved product can never belong to a completely different bank (a different module).

sections.s6_takeaway:
The answer depends on modules. The universal rule is that all permitted subtypes must live in the same module as the sealed type. A sealed hierarchy can never span two different modules, because that would let an external module insert itself into a closed family.

Within a single named module, permitted subtypes may be in different packages. The module is a strong encapsulation boundary, so the author controls everything inside it. In a banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj puts the sealed `Account` interface in an `api` package and the concrete products in a `products` package. Both are in the same `com.bank.accounts` module, so the cross-package permits compiles cleanly. He exports only the `api` package, keeping the products internal.

On the plain classpath (unnamed module), the rule is stricter: all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. Without a module boundary, the package is the only encapsulation unit the compiler can trust. Trying to permit a subtype from another package gives a compile error.

The practical lesson is that modularising unlocks a cleaner package layout for sealed hierarchies while still keeping them strongly closed. The module boundary also means an outside vendor module can never inject a new permitted account type into a sealed `Account`, so the product set stays protected. And because the permitted set is recorded in the class file and re-validated by the JVM at load time, nobody can smuggle in a cross-module subtype through bytecode either.

Remember one sentence: same module, different packages is allowed; classpath requires the same package; different modules is never allowed.
